title: Ivo and the Ledger
premise: In the waning years of a long continental war, Mirabel Dunmore works as a nurse in a military hospital attached to a printing workshop, secretly recording in her ledger the names of soldiers whose deaths officers have struck from official reports. When an unknown woman leaves a child at her door with instructions to forget the face, Mirabel realizes the boy is tied to a name in her ledger—and that someone powerful wants both erased. As she traces the child's identity through forged documents, compromised officers, and the workshop's clandestine presses, she must decide whether to publish the true count of the dead before the war's end and the century's turn destroy the evidence. The novel ends with Mirabel choosing exposure over safety: the ledger is printed and scattered, the workshop burns, and she escapes with the child, carrying memory forward at the cost of everything else.
about_author: Isandro Delacroix is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed military records before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about the people history forgot to count.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Names
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Introduces the hospital ward, the workshop next door, and the ledger hidden beneath her sewing basket as she records a dead private omitted from the morning report. Emotional beat: quiet defiance established; we feel the cost of noticing what others are paid to forget.

chapters.title: Instructions to Forget
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. A rain-soaked night: a woman leaves a boy of about seven at the workshop door, whispers instructions to forget the face, and vanishes. The child clutches a scrap of printed paper bearing a name Mirabel recognizes from her ledger. Beat: dread and reluctant responsibility.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Mirabel and Tobias, the child. Mirabel hides the boy among convalescents while Tobias narrates fragments of his journey—coaches, a river, a man called the Clerk. Beat: tenderness growing alongside fear of discovery.

chapters.title: Colonel Vane's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Vane's POV (antagonist). The colonel reviews casualty figures he has falsified for the War Office and learns a woman at the hospital keeps unusual notes. He orders a discreet inquiry. Beat: cold menace; power revealed as bookkeeping.

chapters.title: What the Presses Know
chapters.summary: Workshop master Aldous Fenwick's POV. Fenwick, once a forger, recognizes the paper scrap as his own stock—printed three winters ago for a client he never saw twice. Beat: guilt resurfacing; the past pressing on the present.

chapters.title: A Ledger of Omissions
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She cross-references the boy's paper with her entries and finds a cluster of nine names, all struck from the rolls the same week—all men of one company that supposedly never fought. Beat: the pattern emerges; curiosity hardens into purpose.

chapters.title: The Company That Never Was
chapters.summary: Sergeant Bracken's POV, a drunk veteran of the phantom company. Mirabel finds him in the taverns; he tells her the company was used for a massacre dressed up as enemy action, then dissolved on paper. Beat: horror; testimony as burden.

chapters.title: Visitors After Dark
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Vane's inquiry arrives as a charming captain, Captain Rook, who flirts and probes. Mirabel performs invisibility while moving the ledger and the boy to the workshop cellar. Beat: cat-and-mouse tension; performance under pressure.

chapters.title: Tobias Remembers
chapters.summary: Tobias's POV. Under Fenwick's gentle questioning with toy soldiers, the boy reconstructs his escape: his father was one of the nine, and his mother—the woman at the door—is still alive, hiding. Beat: heartbreak; the stakes become flesh.

chapters.title: The Clerk of Records
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. We meet the Clerk, the civilian architect of the false company, who warns Vane that loose paper is more dangerous than loose soldiers. Vane begins planning not an investigation but a fire. Beat: conspiracy deepens; villain alliance frays.

chapters.title: Ink Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Fenwick's POV. Fenwick confesses his forging past to Mirabel and offers the presses: they can print the true ledger as a broadsheet before the year ends. Mirabel hesitates—printing means becoming visible forever. Beat: the central choice crystallizes.

chapters.title: Rook's Kindness
chapters.summary: Rook's POV. The captain, genuinely moved by the ward, begins doubting his orders; he discovers a fragment of the ledger but says nothing yet. Beat: moral complication; even the hunter wavers.

chapters.title: The Widow at the Mill
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Following Tobias's clues, Mirabel locates the boy's mother, Livia, hiding at a mill—but Vane's men are watching the road. She must choose between retrieving Livia now or protecting the ledger. Beat: impossible trade-off; survival priced in people.

chapters.title: A Bargain in the Chapel
chapters.summary: Mirabel and Rook's shared POV scene. Rook confronts Mirabel; instead of arresting her, he proposes a bargain—he can delay Vane's report if she gives him the original ledger as insurance. Beat: uneasy trust; betrayal seeded.

chapters.title: What Burns First
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane learns of Rook's hesitation and moves the timeline up: the workshop will burn within the fortnight, officially an accident of lamp oil. Beat: ticking clock installed; dread becomes countdown.

chapters.title: Setting the Type
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, mostly Mirabel and Fenwick. By lamplight the workshop sets the type of the true ledger—nine names, the massacre, the signatures—while Tobias sleeps above. Beat: sacred labor; hope sharpened by imminent loss.

chapters.title: The Night of Lamp Oil
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. Vane's men come early; Rook, unable to fully betray either side, raises just enough alarm. The press run finishes as torches reach the yard. Beat: climax ignites; chaos and courage intertwined.

chapters.title: Ash and Broadside
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The workshop burns; Fenwick stays with his presses and does not come out. Mirabel, Tobias, and Livia flee through the mill stream carrying bundles of the printed broadside. Beat: grief and release; the price of survival paid in full view.

chapters.title: Paper on Every Door
chapters.summary: Bracken's and townsfolk POVs. The broadsides spread through garrison town and capital alike; officers cannot unpublish truth. Vane's arithmetic unravels publicly. Beat: vindication arriving too late to feel like victory.

chapters.title: The Colonel's Reckoning
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Summoned, stripped, scapegoated by the very system he served; the Clerk vanishes without consequence. Vane's final reflection mirrors Mirabel's first entry. Beat: power consuming itself; corruption's banal end.

chapters.title: A New Page
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Spring after the war's end: Mirabel, Tobias, and Livia settle in a river village where she opens a small school and begins a second ledger—not of omissions, but of living names. Beat: quiet healing; memory repurposed as care.

chapters.title: Ivo and the Ledger
chapters.summary: Tobias—Ivo, his true name restored—narrates as an adult, decades later, reading the surviving copy of the broadside to children and explaining the woman who kept the count when no one else would. Beat: legacy; the century turns, and the names remain.
